title: Common Wealth Canada, "BC LVT widget" (five-option summary panel embedded on commonwealth.ca; portal to the "BC Land Value Policy Hub" at /lvt-hub-bc, September 2026)
what_was_fetched: Widget page fetched with curl + browser user-agent (HTTP 200, 373 KB Squarespace page). The widget is inline HTML/JS in a code block (no iframe, no external JSON); the full inline script was extracted and read (all five variants' copy and figures are hard-coded in the script). The linked full page https://www.commonwealth.ca/lvt-hub-bc (HTTP 200, 758 KB) was also fetched: its 14.5K-character prose was read in full and its 185 KB inline data/copy script (BUNDLE of model output, variant parameters, 'bottom line' text, notes) was extracted and searched. The existing /bc-lvt page (Oct 2025 'BC's Big Fix') was re-fetched to see whether it links to the widget or hub (it does not); the commonwealth.ca homepage does not link either page. Both /bc-lvt-widget and /lvt-hub-bc are listed in the site's public sitemap.xml and carry no noindex tag. No author byline, model documentation, technical paper or data download is published on either page. Files in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-georgism-wiki/27113c0d-0e4a-5705-a87d-69e4d8108829/scratchpad/t0-2026-09-30b/ (widget.html, widget-code.html, hub.html, hub.txt, hub-script.js, bclvt.html, sitemap.xml).
verdict: DEFER. The widget is a homepage-bound teaser (the queue note says 'preparing for homepage after demo and review'); the substantive page it points to describes its own results as preliminary from a 'calibrated version' of a model whose documentation and full results are still 'to be published'. The widget's own footnote drops that caveat. Nothing here is a source of findings (Tier 2, advocacy-organisation model output). Re-queue when CWC publishes the technical documentation or a fuller results paper. If the T1 wants something now, the most that is defensible is ONE sentence on organizations/common-wealth-canada.md (Research Program) and none on places/british-columbia.md, describing the resource as a proponent's tool with assumptions stated, e.g.: 'In September 2026 the organisation published an interactive explorer of five British Columbia land-value-return scenarios run through its own dynamic general-equilibrium model, describing the results as preliminary and not final estimates.' Link the hub (/lvt-hub-bc), not the widget URL, as the canonical page; do not reproduce any modelled figure (house-price falls, output gains, poverty effects) on either page.
claim_grade: D (interpretive/modelled projections) from a Tier 2 source (Common Wealth Canada, advocacy organisation; origin/proponent only per EDITORIAL 4c). Usable only as 'the organisation describes...' for the existence and design of the tool.
content_summary:
WHAT IT DOES: a tabbed panel, 'Five ways to return land value to British Columbia', that auto-rotates through five policy variants (stops on click), each showing the policy design, one headline rate line and three 'takes' (Housing / Households / Economy). Nothing is user-adjustable: no sliders, inputs or calculator; all figures are pre-computed and hard-coded. Link 'Explore the full model' goes to /lvt-hub-bc. The hub page adds a 'BC Land Value Tax Explorer' with policy parameters, charts against a no-reform baseline, a regional map across 19 BC Assessment areas, and per-variant 'bottom line' text.
VARIANTS AND HEADLINE FIGURES (CWC's own model output; do not treat as findings): (1) Land Dividend Income: 1.35% on all land, funds a negative income tax ($25,000 per family guarantee, 40% clawback), labour-income tax 28% to 22.6%, raises $14.8B vs costs $14.5B; land prices -22%, median house value -17%, family poverty 10% to 0%, output +1.9%. (2) Slow LVT Transition: 5% terminal rate phased in over 30 years, revenue-neutral, labour-income tax 28% to 16.3%; median house value -39%, +104,200 homes, 70% of households better off, outright owners lose 4.3%, output +3.9%. (3) Maximalist / Full LVT Shift: 10% on land, building tax abolished, labour-income tax to 13.8%, revenue-neutral; land prices -68%, median house value -52%, +245,700 homes, output +5.0%, consumption +7.9%, legacy loan-to-value 0.80 to 1.48 ('needs transition protection'). (4) Landlords' Tax: 2.5% on non-principal-residence land, income tax 28% to 25.1%; +22,700 homes, output +1.1%, house values +0.6%. (5) Progressive Land Wealth Tax: 5% above a large household exemption; 99.97% of residential land exempt so it raises essentially nothing; output 0.0%, 94.5% better off.
ASSUMPTIONS AND DATA NAMED: 'Common Wealth BC land value tax model (V13C)', 'a dynamic general equilibrium model of the province'. Household side is 30 representative groups (ten income deciles x renters / mortgaged owners / outright owners), not microdata. Baseline: 2025 BC Assessment roll totals (regional map); 2021 Census occupied dwellings by tenure (1,363,190 owner-occupied, 669,450 renter-occupied) used only to convert modelled stock percentages into dwelling counts; benchmark median BC house price $929,619 at a 76% median land share; the labour-income tax rate is 'a stylized model rate, not the B.C. statutory schedule'; 'better off' means lifetime consumption-equivalent welfare. The hub says results are 'preliminary', produced 'with a calibrated version of the model before the final work with the full research dataset', 'not final empirical results' and 'not... a forecast'; it says technical documentation and fuller results will follow. Elasticities, capitalisation/cap-rate assumptions and calibration targets are not stated.
WHO BUILT IT: Common Wealth Canada; no named author on either page (site footer/menus only). The wiki's CWC page lists Liam Wilkinson (Research and Policy) as the modeller of its earlier distributional study; that attribution is NOT made on these pages.
existing_wiki_coverage: organizations/common-wealth-canada.md (Research Program) covers the 2023 flagship rent report, the 2024 distributional-impacts and price-reaction papers, the BC history blog, 'B.C.'s Big Fix' (/bc-lvt, updated Oct 2025) and two Jack Jol notes; it says nothing about a five-variant model, the /lvt-hub-bc page or V13C. places/british-columbia.md ('Recent Fiscal Proposals...') states the Oct 2025 Big Fix scenarios (LVT ~0.8% replacing property taxes/SVT/PTT, ~$12B, house prices -16%; ~1.8% also replacing provincial income taxes, house prices -40%) as 'advocacy-stage projections'. The new hub's numbers are from a different, newer model run and are NOT reconciled with those (e.g. 5% LVT gives a 39% median house-value fall; 10% gives 52%); adding any of them to the BC page would create an unexplained internal inconsistency. research/cwc-distributional-impacts-lvt.md and research/cwc-lvt-price-reaction-model.md (national-level, 2024) are the closest existing research pages.
uncertainties: (1) Status: the queue note says the widget is 'preparing for homepage after demo and review', i.e. it may change before launch; the hub is public and indexed but self-labelled preliminary. (2) Widget footnote says 'All figures are output from the Common Wealth BC land value tax model' without the hub's 'preliminary' caveat, so the widget alone overstates finality. (3) Widget copy is not identical to hub copy (e.g. widget 'Landlords' Tax' labels; hub static markup contains a leftover 'Split-Rate Property Tax Shift' placeholder label as option 01 before the script replaces it): minor, but shows the page is still being edited. (4) The widget's dwelling counts (+104,200, +245,700, +22,700) are the site's own conversion of modelled percentages using 2021 Census tenure counts, not a model output. (5) Rent effects are counter-intuitive (rents end 5-7% higher under the revenue-neutral shifts); the page flags this but without a stated mechanism, so a T1 must not paraphrase. (6) Editorial-independence note: the wiki's CWC page names Floyd Marinescu as founder; keep the treatment strictly to the Tier 2 'origin/proponent' rubric and consider whether the T1 wants to leave the decision to another editor. (7) No public methodology, code or data was found, so nothing can be independently checked.

title: Taxpayers for Common Sense (Autumn Hanna et al.), "Royalty Rip-Off: How below-market federal oil and gas royalty rates cost taxpayers $25 billion over a decade", report, 23 September 2026 (7 pp)
what_was_fetched: FULL TEXT read. Landing page and companion press release (/century-old-oil-and-gas-royalty-rate-costs-taxpayers-billions/) fetched with curl + browser user-agent (both HTTP 200). Report PDF https://www.taxpayer.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Royalty-Rip-Off.pdf downloaded (HTTP 200, 954 KB, 7 pages) and parsed with pymupdf; all 7 pages including the 27 endnotes read (page numbers below are PDF pages = printed pages; the charts on p.3 are images and have no text layer, so the state bar values in the chart were not read, only the text). Primary sources chased: GAO-17-540 (June 2017): direct curl and browser UA returned 403 (Akamai), r.jina.ai returned text, and the Googlebot user-agent returned the full 36-page PDF, parsed with pymupdf and read pp.1-2, 16-24 (report pp. 16-24 + highlights). CBO 'Options for Increasing Federal Income From Crude Oil and Natural Gas on Federal Lands' (April 2016; cbo.gov/publication/51421 and the PDF): NOT FETCHED - HTTP 403 with a DataDome CAPTCHA to curl (browser UA and Googlebot UA), r.jina.ai (CAPTCHA warning), and WebFetch; Wayback not reachable from this environment. CBO content below is therefore taken second-hand from GAO-17-540 (quoting CBO) and from a search-result summary of the CBO page. Statute: 30 U.S.C. 226 and 43 U.S.C. 1337 fetched from law.cornell.edu (HTTP 200), amendment notes read; uscode.house.gov 30 U.S.C. 226 also fetched but it is an older text without the 2025 notes. BLM Final RIA 2024 and ONRR federal-sales data were not fetched (ONRR revenuedata page returned the landing page only, no dataset parsed; BLM press URL 404). Files in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-georgism-wiki/27113c0d-0e4a-5705-a87d-69e4d8108829/scratchpad/t0-2026-09-30b/ (report.txt, royalty-rip-off.pdf, gao-17-540.txt, gao-17-540-gb.pdf, tcs.txt, tcs-news.txt, cornell226.html, cornell43-1337.html).
verdict: NEW research/gao-2017-federal-royalty-rates.md (GAO-17-540, 'Oil, Gas, and Coal Royalties: Raising Federal Rates Could Decrease Production on Federal Lands but Increase Federal Revenue', June 2017): a Tier 1 official-body report, 36 pages, readable, with a mixed finding that is more useful to the wiki than the watchdog's summary of it. Pair it with ENRICH concepts/resource-rents.md (a short 'US federal onshore royalties' subsection: the statutory timeline below, GAO's finding, and the point that a flat gross-revenue royalty is not a rent tax and can bite marginal wells, linking to the existing Gaffney/Mintz-Chen pages) and a one-line ENRICH of benefits/resource-rent-capture-works.md 'Honest Scope' (federal US royalty is a case where rent capture is hard to raise ex-post because rates lock in at lease issue). Do NOT create a page on the TCS report; cite TCS only as 'the budget watchdog Taxpayers for Common Sense (Tier 2, advocacy/oversight group), which released a report on 23 September 2026 arguing...' inside a Current-debate or Who-promotes-it position, as origin of the 'rip-off' framing and of the $25bn retroactive estimate, with its status stated, never in the lead. Facts must be cited to the statute (Pub. L. 117-169 s.50262; Pub. L. 119-21 s.50101/50102), GAO-17-540 and, once accessible, CBO 51421 and ONRR/BLM, not to TCS. CBO cannot be treated as read: keep CBO statements only as 'GAO reports that CBO concluded...' until the CBO document is opened by someone who can reach it.
claim_grade: TCS report: B (empirical/counterfactual estimate) from a Tier 2 source (nonpartisan-labelled budget watchdog, advocacy for reform; origin/proponent only). GAO-17-540: A/B from a Tier 1 official body (GAO), read directly. Statute: A from Tier 1 (US Code). CBO 2016: B, Tier 1, NOT read directly (second-hand via GAO).
content_summary:
TCS REPORT CLAIMS (page numbers = PDF pages):
- p.1 and p.3: federal and state taxpayers would have received about $25 billion more in 2016-2025 had an 18.75% royalty rate applied to federal onshore oil and gas; record $4.6 billion in 2022 alone (p.1; press release).
- METHOD (p.3, fn 7-8, p.6): ONRR reported $47 billion of royalties collected on $402 billion of oil and gas sold from federal lands, 2016-2025 (ONRR 'Federal sales' data, accessed 5 Aug 2026). TCS applies 18.75% to those sales and subtracts $3.4 billion of approved allowances (fn 8: effective rate over the period was 11.7%, below the 12.5% statutory minimum, 'largely due to' those allowances). T0 recomputation: 0.1875 x 402 - 3.4 - 47 = 24.97, i.e. about $25bn; so the figure is a static, retroactive, all-leases counterfactual: same sales volumes and prices, no production or bidding response, applied to leases already issued at 12.5% or 16.67% (rates fixed at issue; the report notes new rates apply only to leases issued after enactment, p.2). Split $12.4bn federal and $12.4bn states (p.3) because roughly half goes to the producing state (p.2 fn 2: states 49%, Reclamation Fund 40%, Permit Processing Improvement Fund 1%, Treasury 10%; Alaska 88% to the state). By state (p.3): New Mexico $16.2bn total ($8.1bn state share), Wyoming $2.1bn (state share, as the text is ambiguous), North Dakota $887m, Colorado $481m, Utah $322m.
- RATE HISTORY (p.2, fn 3-6): Mineral Leasing Act 1920 set a 12.5% statutory minimum; unchanged for over a century until raised to 16.67% in August 2022 (Inflation Reduction Act); in July 2025 lowered again to a 12.5% minimum for new leases; TCS estimates a $1.5bn loss over the next decade from that reversal (fn 6, TCS's own 'By the Numbers' page). BLM's 2024 Final RIA projected $12.7bn for federal and state taxpayers 2023-2042 from the 2022 terms ($2.3bn 2023-31, $10.4bn 2032-42). BLM has used its authority to charge more than the minimum only once, in a 2022 lease sale (p.3, fn 9). DOI Inspector General (June 2023): average effective onshore rate 2016-2020 was 0.49 points below the legal minimum for oil and 2.58 points for gas (p.2, fn 3). 2025 onshore program revenue $7.2bn, of which royalties $6.9bn (96%) (p.2, fn 1).
- STATE COMPARISON (p.3, fns 10-21; chart of rates not text-extractable): Texas typically 20-25% on state lands (fn 18: 12.5% minimum on state lands, 20-25% minimum on public school lands); New Mexico 18.75-25% (fn 14, SB 23, April 2025); Colorado, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Utah, Wyoming 'commonly' 16.67-20%; Alaska 12.5% minimum, generally 16.67%; Louisiana 12.5% minimum, generally 20-25%; Pennsylvania 12.5% minimum, generally 20% for leases after 2018; also California, West Virginia, Ohio cited without stated rates. Note the state 'minimums' in several fns are 12.5%, so the comparison is of typical/generally-charged rates, not statutory floors. 1987: DOI cited the 12.5% rate on state and private lands to justify keeping the federal rate (p.3-4, fn 23).
- OFFSHORE (p.4): Bush administration raised offshore rates 2006-2008; DOI found Gulf of Mexico lease demand stayed strong after the rise from 16.67% to 18.75% in 2008 (fn 26, GAO-14-50); 'in 2025, Congress lowered the rates for new offshore leases to between 12.5% and 16.7%, down from a minimum of 16.67% and a maximum of 18.75%'. Statute check (43 U.S.C. 1337(a)(1) amendment notes, LII): IRA s.50261 had set 16 2/3% to 18 3/4% for 10 years from 16 Aug 2022 and not less than 16 2/3% thereafter; Pub. L. 119-21 s.50102(d) repealed that and set 'not less than 12 1/2 percent, but not more than 16 2/3 percent'. This matches TCS.
- PRODUCTION CLAIMS (p.4): CBO estimated raising the onshore rate to 18.75% would raise 'roughly $400 million for federal and state taxpayers over the first decade' with a 'negligible' production effect (fn 24, CBO April 2016); GAO 'reached similar conclusions, finding that raising federal royalty rates would increase federal revenue while reducing production on federal lands by a small amount or not at all' (fn 25, GAO June 2017). Market evidence: Texas 25% on new state leases for 30+ years; Utah SITLA 16.67% in 2008; Colorado 16.67% (2011) then 20% (2016); average BLM bids $2,149/acre (2023) and $1,085 (2024) vs $288 average 2013-2022 (fn 27, TCS's own analysis). Recommendations (p.5): Congress raise the minimum to 18.75%; or Interior act by rule or lease-by-lease.

TIER 1 VERIFICATION DONE BY T0:
- Statute (LII, 30 U.S.C. 226 notes): Pub. L. 117-169 s.50262(a)(1)(B) (16 Aug 2022) substituted '16 2/3 percent' for '12 1/2 per centum' and was repealed by Pub. L. 119-21 s.50101(a)(1) (4 July 2025), 'as if those subsections had not been enacted'. So the onshore rate history is: 12.5% (1920 to Aug 2022) -> 16.67% (Aug 2022 to July 2025) -> 12.5% (from 4 July 2025). The queue note's 'stuck at 1920 minimum' is therefore imprecise: it was raised for 35 months and then reversed; and the 12.5% statutory minimum is the same as in 1920.
- GAO-17-540 (June 2017, Frank Rusco, GAO Natural Resources and Environment; no recommendations): Highlights p.2: raising rates 'could decrease oil, gas, and coal production on federal lands but increase overall federal revenue, according to studies GAO reviewed and stakeholders interviewed. However, the extent of these effects is uncertain and depends, according to stakeholders, on several other factors, such as market conditions and prices.' Production: one study found oil and gas production 'could decrease by less than 2 percent per year' if rates rose from 12.5% to 22.5%; another said the effect 'could be "negligible" over 10 years' at 18.75%. Report p.16: 'Both studies suggested that a higher royalty rate could decrease production on federal lands by either a small amount or not at all' (the two studies being CBO 2016 and Enegis LLC 2011 for BLM); GAO quotes CBO: raising to 18.75% 'would lead to "reductions in production [that] would be small or even negligible" over 10 years, particularly if the increased federal royalty rate remained equal to or below the royalty rates for production on state or private lands.' Enegis modelled oil declines of 0 to ~70 million barrels over 25 years (about 1.8% of FY2016 onshore federal oil per year) and gas 0 to 85 bcf (under 1% per year); no change only where companies fully absorb the cost. Revenue: oil and gas studies estimated net federal revenue gains of $5 million to $38 million per year; Enegis: $125 million to $939 million over 25 years for 16.67%/18.75%/22.5%. Caveats (pp.19-20, 23-24): effects apply only to new leases and would begin within the first 10 years (p.16 fn 44); lower bonus bids might offset royalty gains (oil and gas bonus bids were 8% of FY2016 federal onshore oil and gas revenue); effects fall mainly on marginal wells at low prices (citing CRS 2015); oil cost increase from 12.5% to 16.67% about $2 a barrel at March 2017 prices. GAO also notes state oil and gas rates 'tend to be higher than federal royalty rates' in the six states with over 90% of federal production (Highlights).
- CBO 'Options for Increasing Federal Income From Crude Oil and Natural Gas on Federal Lands' (April 2016): title, date and URL confirmed via GAO and a search result; a search-result summary of the CBO page says raising the onshore rate to 18.75% to match offshore would generate '$200 million in net federal income over the next 10 years'. TCS's '$400 million for federal and state' is consistent with that if the state share roughly doubles it but T0 could NOT confirm; treat as unverified.

URLS: CBO https://www.cbo.gov/publication/51421 and https://www.cbo.gov/sites/default/files/114th-congress-2015-2016/reports/51421-oil_and_gas_options-OneCol-3.pdf; GAO-17-540 https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-17-540.pdf (product page https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-17-540); GAO-14-50 (Dec 2013, 'Oil and Gas Resources: Actions Needed for Interior to Better Ensure a Fair Return') https://www.gao.gov/products/GAO-14-50; DOI OIG June 2023 'The U.S. Department of the Interior Does Not Analyze Effective Royalty Rates' (link in TCS fn 3); BLM Final RIA 1004-AE80 (4.9.24) https://www.regulations.gov/document/BLM-2023-0005-130198; ONRR federal sales https://revenuedata.onrr.gov/downloads/federal-sales/.
existing_wiki_coverage: None on the US federal onshore royalty regime: no grep hit in the corpus digest or the repo for 'Mineral Leasing Act', ONRR, Inflation Reduction Act royalty, Taxpayers for Common Sense, taxpayer.net or GAO-17-540. Closest existing pages: research/gaffney-mineral-leasing-tax-reform.md (Gaffney on Canadian crown-land leasing errors and US federal oil tax loopholes, 1970s-2000s essays), research/gaffney-alaska-oil-leasing.md (1977 Alaska ad valorem charge; ranks it above bonus bidding and flat royalties), concepts/resource-rents.md (sections 'Severance Tax Design and Incidence', 'Leasing-Based Rent Capture', 'Two Institutional Channels for Rent Leakage'; See Also lists Australia PRRT, India MMDR ruling, NZ royalty review) and benefits/resource-rent-capture-works.md (Norway, Botswana, Alaska 1977, Montana coal, 'Honest Scope'). research/mintz-chen-capturing-resource-rents.md (Calgary SPP; 'the optimal royalty is a rent-based one') is the natural theory link: a flat percentage-of-value royalty like the federal one is not a rent tax, which the GAO caveats on marginal wells illustrate. Any new page needs at least 2 inbound links (resource-rents, gaffney-mineral-leasing-tax-reform or mintz-chen are natural).
uncertainties: (1) CBO 2016 was not opened (CAPTCHA); the $400m/first-decade and 'negligible' figures are second-hand (GAO quote for 'negligible'; a search summary gave $200m net federal). Someone with access should read CBO 51421 and the budget-option page 51505 before any CBO number is published. (2) The $25bn is a hypothetical retroactive static estimate; it should not be described as 'foregone' revenue in the wiki's own voice, and it is not comparable with the forward-looking CBO ($200-400m/decade) or GAO ($5-38m/yr) figures, which apply only to new leases and include some production response and bonus-bid effects. TCS does not reconcile the two orders of magnitude. (3) TCS's paraphrase of GAO ('increase revenue with little or no effect on production') drops GAO's headline that production 'could decrease' and its stakeholder caveats; GAO itself reports the 'small amount or not at all' as what two studies suggested, one of which (Enegis) shows declines in nearly every scenario and falling lease demand. (4) The TCS 'no evidence that raising the rate to 16.67% decreased leasing' rests on TCS's own bid data for 2023-24 (fn 27), confounded by the 2022 price spike and the IRA's other changes; treat as TCS's inference. (5) State rates are TCS's summary of typical rates from statutes and sample leases; T0 spot-checked none of the state statutes. Several footnotes show 12.5% state minimums, so 'almost all states charge more' is about generally-charged rates. (6) The 2022 rate applied to leases issued after 16 Aug 2022; the 2025 reversal (Pub. L. 119-21 s.50101, 4 July 2025) applies to new leases; T0 did not check transition provisions or the exact 30 U.S.C. 226(b)(1)(A) current text (the LII page shows only amendment notes; confirm on uscode.house.gov/govinfo). (7) Autumn Hanna is credited in the press release as vice president of TCS; the PDF names no authors. (8) The queue's 'nonpartisan budget watchdog' is TCS's own self-description; under 4c it is Tier 2. (9) 2016-2025 covers a period in which the rate was 12.5% for most leases and 16.67% for leases from Aug 2022; the 18.75% counterfactual is therefore partly measured against a rate that was already higher on new leases.
